Respiratory Therapist here. I have been working in ICU's for close to 30years.

Ventilators are used to improve oxygenation and ventilation.

Oxygenation is a measure of the hemoglobin that is saturated with oxygen, it is controlled by the FiO2(Fraction of inspired oxygen) delivered and also something called PEEP(positive end expiratory pressure)

PEEP is the pressure that is maintained in the lungs at the end of the expiratory phase, this pressure prevents atelectasis (Opens the little air sacks in your lungs) As you increase the PEEP your patients oxygenation will improve.

Ventilation is the removal of CO2, it is controlled by the size of the breath delivered called the Vt (tidal volume) and the RR(respiratory rate)

There are many different modes but the 2 most commonly used is Pressure control and Volume Control.

In pressure control you set a pressure to achieve a specific Vt, usually 6-10 cc's / kilograms of body weight

In volume control you set a Volume that determines the size of the breath, 6-10 cc's / kg body weight

I pressure control the pressure is constant but the volume can vary.

In volume control the volume is constant but the pressure can vary

As a patients lung compliance changes, the volume and pressure needs to be adjusted or you will under ventilate the patient and the CO2 will rise, or if you hyperventilate the patient driving the CO2 below normal values.

Normal level for CO2 is 35-45 mmgh, as the CO2 rises the patient becomes acidotic, when its to low patient becomes alkalotic.

Low Co2 is called hypocarbia and can cause blood to diverted away from the brain resulting in seizure activity.

High CO2 is called hypercarbia, it causes acidosis and can cause lethargy(unresponsiveness)

These blood gasses are measured in a blood gas analyzer. We draw a blood sample from the patient, pop it in the machine, pops out the results. Most blood gas analyzers measure PH, PO2, CO2, Hemoglobin, Lactate, Na, Cl, Ca, K+ and glucose. HCO3 and base excess are calculated based on the PH and CO2.

There are some diseases that are called Non-PEEPable lung disorders.

You have something called V/Q ratio, V/Q stands for ventilation/perfusion

You may have some portions of the lungs that are receiving adequate ventilation but has poor perfusion and vise versa.

So as you turn up your PEEP you are opening all the little air sacs(Alveoli) but by doing so you are putting pressure on the capillary bed which can divert blood away from the alveoli. So you end up with a V/Q mismatch.

So in situations with a patient that has poor oxygenation you turn up your oxygen to 100% and increase your PEEP till the oxygenation starts to improve. Most common practice is to continue increasing your PEEP so you can get your Oxygen down to 50%, anything above 50% over a extended period of time can cause O2 toxicity. O2 toxicity causes 3 things, decrease in surfactant production, nitrogen washout and release of free radicals. Oxygen crosses the Alveolar capillary membrane, nitrogen does not, the remaining nitrogen in the alveoli keeps it open. If all you have is 100% oxygen in the alveoli you can end up with atelectasis and cause a V/Q mismatch.

So if these covid patients have poor oxygenation, they may decide to turn the PEEP up and continue turning it up until it elicits a response. Once you get to PEEP levels of 20-25cm/H2O, you are increasing the chance for barotrauma(lung damage from high pressures) and you get things like pneumothorax.

I read that in covid patients the virus was causing the iron in the hemoglobin to separate from the heme. The iron was collecting in the capillaries in the lungs causing more of a perfusion problem, not a issue that can be corrected with a ventilator. So chances are the doctors were going up on pressures and continued increasing pressures to dangerous levels and it was not working, in fact it could have made things worse.
Then the next thing is getting weaned off those things, right? I do not specialize in that area, but am aware of that common hurdle.

Ya, you have to get the FIO2 down to 40%, PEEP down to 5, then you start weaning the respiratory rate. Once you get the rate down to 5 you can pull the endotube if the gasses look ok. There are some things we do called weaning parameters, one is called a rapid shallow breathing index, also NIF and VC(negative inspiratory force and vital capacity. Tells us how strong your respiratory muscles are.

You see, what happens is once a patient is placed on those high ventilating pressures a doctor might be hesitant to wean those pressures if the blood gasses indicate the patient is not ready. Traditionally, the blood gases will improve, the numbers will get above normal levels, this gives you room to wean the vent. If the numbers are low, they will not wean the vent.
